scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Some data belongs to the whole class, some to each object. Mixing them up causes a famous bug.

scenes.onScreen: "Shared or private?": three numbered lines (1. Class attribute: written in the class body, shared by all; 2. Instance attribute: self.x, private to one object; 3. A shared list is shared by everyone) and an analogy card: a school notice board that everyone sees, versus each student's private notebook
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Data can live in two places. A class attribute is written directly in the class body. All objects share it. Think of a school notice board that everyone can see. An instance attribute is set with self dot, inside init. Each object has its own copy, like a private notebook. Numbers and strings are safe either way, because assigning replaces them. But a list stored on the class is one single list, shared by every object. That is where the trouble starts.

scenes.onScreen: shared.py: a class attribute shared by all dogs, and a list that is shared too
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A Dog class. [HL 2] Species is a class attribute. All dogs share it. [HL 3] So is tricks, one single list. [HL 5] Init gives each dog its own name. That one is private. [HL 8] Learn appends a trick to the tricks list. [HL 11] Rex. [HL 12] Fido. [HL 13] Rex learns to sit. [HL 14] Fido learns to roll. [HL 15] Look at the list through Rex. [HL 16] And through Fido. [HL 17] Both dogs say Canis. [HL 18] The list has sit and roll, even though Rex only learned sit. [HL 19] And it is the very same list. True.

code.source:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis"
    tricks = []

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def learn(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)

d1 = Dog("Rex")
d2 = Dog("Fido")
d1.learn("sit")
d2.learn("roll")
t1 = d1.tricks
t2 = d2.tricks
print(d1.species, d2.species)
print(t1)
print(t1 is t2)

scenes.onScreen: The names t1 and t2 tied to the very same list object
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The names t1 and t2 look like two lists, but they are two names tied to one single list object. That is why the tricks of Rex show up for Fido too. When two names are tied to one object, changing it through one name changes it for both. Remember this picture. It explains the whole bug.

scenes.onScreen: private.py: create the list inside init
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The same Dog class. [HL 2] Species stays a class attribute, because it really is shared. [HL 5] Init sets the name. [HL 6] And now builds a brand new list for each dog. [HL 9] Learn appends to this dog's own list. [HL 11] Rex. [HL 12] Fido. [HL 13] Rex learns sit. [HL 14] Fido learns roll. [HL 15] Rex has only sit. [HL 16] Fido has only roll. [HL 17] And the two lists are different objects. False.

code.source:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.tricks = []

    def learn(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)

d1 = Dog("Rex")
d2 = Dog("Fido")
d1.learn("sit")
d2.learn("roll")
print(d1.tricks)
print(d2.tricks)
print(d1.tricks is d2.tricks)

scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: A class attribute is written in the class body and shared by all objects. Two: An instance attribute is set with self dot inside init, and is private. Three: A list in the class body is one list shared by everyone. Four: Create lists inside init, so each object gets its own. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

class Team:
    members = []

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def add(self, person):
        self.members.append(person)

red = Team("Red")
blue = Team("Blue")
red.add("Asha")
blue.add("Ravi")
print(red.members)
bug.error:
Python output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

['Asha', 'Ravi']
bug.fixed:
class Team:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.members = []

    def add(self, person):
        self.members.append(person)

red = Team("Red")
blue = Team("Blue")
red.add("Asha")
blue.add("Ravi")
print(red.members)
bug.why: A list created in the class body is built once and shared by every object. A list created in init is built fresh for each object.

pun: "Why did the list refuse to be shared? It had too many members already."
challenge: Write a Student class where every student has a list of grades. Make sure two students do not share one list. Prove it with the is operator.
challengeAnswer: Create self.grades = [] inside __init__. Then s1.grades is s2.grades prints False.

shorts.hook: "A class attribute is written in the class body."
shorts.script: A class attribute is written in the class body. Every object shares it. Think of a notice board in school that everyone can read. If you change it on the class, every object sees the change. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Class attributes are shared.

shorts.title: Instance attribute
shorts.hook: "An instance attribute is set with self dot, inside init."
shorts.script: An instance attribute is set with self dot, inside init. Each object gets its own copy. Think of a private notebook. Rex's name does not change Fido's name. Put the data that differs between objects here. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Instance attributes are private.

shorts.title: Shared list
shorts.script: Here is the trap. A list written in the class body is one single list. Every object shares it. Add Asha through one object, and she appears in every object. Two names, one list. The memory picture shows it clearly. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Watch for shared lists.

shorts.title: The fix
shorts.hook: "To give every object its own list, create the list inside init."
shorts.script: To give every object its own list, create the list inside init. Write self dot members equals empty brackets. Python runs init once for each object, so every object builds a fresh list. Now adding a member only changes one object. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Make lists in init.
